title: Micah's Shrine and the Hired Levite
summary: A man named Micah returns eleven hundred shekels of silver he stole from his mother, and she uses part of it to have an idol made for the LORD. Micah sets up a household shrine with an ephod and household gods and makes one of his sons a priest. When a wandering Levite from Bethlehem arrives, Micah hires him as his priest and assumes that the LORD will now bless him.
story: With Samson's death, the stories of the judges end. Chapters 17-21 form an epilogue with no judges and no foreign enemies, only Israel doing what seems right to itself. These chapters are probably not later in time than the Samson story (chapter 20 mentions Phinehas, the grandson of Aaron, which points to an earlier period), but they are placed here to show the religious and moral condition that lay beneath the cycles of the judges. The first story, told in chapters 17-18, concerns worship. It begins in a single household in Ephraim, with theft, a curse, and an idol, and it will end with a whole tribe adopting that idol. The refrain that first appears in 17:6, that there was no king in Israel and everyone did what was right in his own eyes, sets the key for the rest of the book.
historical:
The story is set in the hill country of Ephraim, the same central region where Shiloh, the site of the tabernacle, was located (18:31). The Levites were the tribe set apart for service at the sanctuary. They received no territorial allotment but were given forty-eight towns scattered among the tribes (Joshua 21), and they depended on the tithes and offerings of the people (Numbers 18:21-24; Deuteronomy 18:1-8). Within the tribe of Levi, only the descendants of Aaron were to serve as priests at the altar. A Levite who wandered in search of a living suggests that the system of support was breaking down, perhaps because Israel was neglecting its tithes.

Bethlehem in Judah was not one of the Levitical towns listed in Joshua 21, which makes the young man's residence there as a sojourner another sign that things were not ordered as the law intended. Bethlehem appears again in chapter 19 and in Ruth, and some interpreters see these references as part of the book's quiet interest in the town that would produce King David.
cultural:
Curses spoken over stolen property were believed to have real power, which may explain why Micah confesses once he hears his mother's curse. Her response, blessing her son in the LORD's name and dedicating silver to the LORD to make an idol, shows how thoroughly Israel's faith had mixed with the practices of its neighbors. The second commandment forbade making any carved image for worship (Exodus 20:4-5), and Deuteronomy 27:15 calls down a curse on the one who makes a carved or cast idol and sets it up in secret.

The items in Micah's shrine are known from the Old Testament and the ancient Near East. The graven image and molten idol may be one object (a carved image covered in cast metal) or two. An ephod was a priestly garment, and in some passages an object used to seek guidance from God (Gideon had made one that became a snare in 8:27). Teraphim were household gods, small figures kept in the home, perhaps associated with family ancestors or used in divination; Rachel stole her father's teraphim in Genesis 31. The payment Micah offers, ten shekels a year, clothing, and food, was a respectable salary for the time.
literary: The chapter is short and heavy with irony. Micah's name means who is like the LORD, and in the early verses it appears in a longer form that includes the divine name, yet his house is full of idols. His mother blesses him in the LORD's name for returning stolen silver, dedicates the silver to the LORD, and then keeps most of it. Micah ordains his own son, then replaces him with a Levite, as if a better credential would improve the arrangement. The chapter ends with Micah's confident statement, “Now I know that the LORD will be good to me, because a Levite has become my priest” (17:13), which the reader recognizes as a misunderstanding of the LORD. The narrator's single comment is placed at the center of the chapter in 17:6, explaining everything around it.

outline.t: Micah returns the stolen silver, and his mother has an idol made
Micah's shrine, and the refrain: no king in Israel
A young Levite from Bethlehem becomes Micah's priest

doctrines.note: Micah's household worships the LORD through an image, a priest of its own choosing, and a private shrine. The chapter shows that idolatry is not only worship of other gods but also worship of the true God on one's own terms.

Almost every act in the chapter breaks the law given at Sinai: theft, cursing, carving images, private shrines, and a non-Aaronic priesthood. Doing right in one's own eyes has replaced the covenant's teaching.

The refrain that there was no king in Israel points to a need for rule and order. Read in the context of the whole Old Testament, the longing is not only for a human king but for one who would lead Israel in faithfulness to God.

words.note: Pesel, a carved image or idol, usually of wood or stone. The same word is used in the second commandment (Exodus 20:4). Micah's mother dedicates it to the LORD, but its very existence breaks the covenant. It will be the object stolen and carried off in chapter 18.

Teraphim, household gods. The word appears several times in the Old Testament, including in the stories of Rachel (Genesis 31) and Michal (1 Samuel 19). Their precise function is debated, but they were associated with the household and perhaps with divination. Their presence in Micah's shrine shows the mixture of Israelite and Canaanite practice.

Yashar, right or upright. The refrain that everyone did what was right in his own eyes turns a word that usually describes what is right in the LORD's eyes (Deuteronomy 12:25, 28) into a description of moral self-rule. The shift from God's eyes to one's own eyes sums up the book's last chapters.

Ephod, a priestly garment. The high priest's ephod held the breastpiece with the Urim and Thummim, used to seek God's will (Exodus 28). Outside the sanctuary, an ephod could become an object of misplaced trust, as with Gideon's in 8:27 and Micah's here.

christ: Micah wanted a priest who would secure God's favor, and he thought a Levite for hire would do. The New Testament presents Jesus as the true priest who cannot be hired or controlled, one appointed by God himself, not by human choice (Hebrews 5:4-6). He does not serve a private shrine but has entered the true sanctuary in heaven on behalf of his people (Hebrews 9:24). The chapter also sharpens the longing expressed in its refrain. The need for a king who would lead Israel in right worship grows through Judges and Samuel and is partly met by David. Christians confess that it is fully met in Jesus, the Son of David, who calls for worship in spirit and truth (John 4:23-24). The link is thematic; the chapter shows a need, not a prediction.

hard.q: Why does the book say there was no king, and is it arguing that a monarchy would solve Israel's problems?
hard.a: The refrain appears four times in the epilogue (17:6, 18:1, 19:1, 21:25), twice in the full form that adds everyone did what was right in his own eyes. Many scholars read it as pro-monarchy, written or edited in the time of the kings to show why Israel needed one, perhaps specifically David's line, since Bethlehem appears favorably and Gibeah (Saul's hometown) appears badly. Others note that the kings of Israel and Judah often led the people into the same idolatry, which the books of Kings record, so the refrain cannot mean that any king would solve the problem. Some read the refrain as a longing for the LORD's own kingship, which Gideon had affirmed in 8:23 and which the people had rejected. Many interpreters hold these together: the book shows the chaos of a people without leadership, while the rest of Scripture shows that only a righteous king who rules under God can bring the order they need.

questions: Micah's mother dedicated silver to the LORD and used it to make an idol. Where do people today mix sincere devotion with ways of worship God has not asked for?
Micah thought having the right priest would guarantee God's blessing. How do people try to secure God's favor through religious credentials or practices?
What does it mean in your life to do what is right in your own eyes, and what would it mean to do what is right in God's eyes?
